title: Fremont County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fremont County wells have a median depth of 182 ft and yield of 7 gpm. Review local drilling costs, water levels and risks before buying land.
h1: Wells and Drilling Costs in Fremont County
intro_html:
A well near Cotopaxi is not a reliable cost guide for a lot in Penrose. Fremont County covers varied mountain ground, and finding usable water depends on the geology beneath the parcel, not just the county average.

Colorado DWR records include 10,255 permitted wells in Fremont County, with 6,637 recorded as constructed. Reported wells have a median depth of 182 ft and median pump yield of 7.0 gpm. Those figures help frame a purchase or drilling budget, but nearby completion reports are the better starting point for a specific property.

sections.heading: Why Fremont County Well Depths Spread So Widely
sections.html:
Of the 7,003 wells reporting depth, the median is 182 ft, with the middle half between 80 and 320 ft. That spread matters more to a drilling bid than the median alone: a quote built around the county midpoint may leave substantial additional footage to pay for.

The permit aquifer field groups 10,026 wells as unnamed or fractured bedrock, while 54 name Alluvial and 19 name Dakota. In fractured granite and gneiss, a driller is looking for water-bearing fractures, and neighboring holes can perform differently.

The depth distribution reaches 500 ft at the 90th percentile, and 6% fall in the 600+ ft category. Compare nearby logs around Howard, Coaldale or your actual building site before choosing a budget depth.

sections.heading: What a 7.0 Gpm Fremont County Well Can Tell You
sections.html:
Reported pump yields cluster in a useful range for household planning: the median is 7.0 gpm, and the middle half runs from 4.5 to 10.0 gpm. Among the 3,276 wells with yield reports, 61% fall in the 5–15 gpm category. A reported drilling yield, however, is not a guarantee of sustained supply under daily use.

The 3% reporting under 1 gpm deserve particular attention from buyers. A low-producing well may require storage and careful demand management; have its pumping performance and recovery evaluated before closing.

Also check what the permit allows. Domestic/household use appears on 83% of county records, but household permission should not be treated as permission for irrigation or every planned outdoor use.

sections.heading: Fremont Water Levels Are Deeper in Recent Records
sections.html:
Static water level is where water stands in a resting well, not the bottom of the drilled hole. Fremont County's 827 reported static levels have a median depth to water of 85 ft, with the middle half between 50 and 160 ft below ground.

Decade medians were 38 ft in the 1970s, 45 ft in the 1980s, 90 ft in the 1990s, 85 ft in the 2000s, 80 ft in the 2010s and 100 ft in the 2020s. Recent records show deeper median water levels than early records, but the pattern is not a steady decline.

These are different groups of measurements, not repeat readings from the same wells. They suggest a concern worth investigating, not proof that the water level beneath a particular Florence or Cotopaxi parcel is dropping.

sections.heading: Fremont's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
Fremont County's largest permit decade was the 1990s, with 2,460 permits, followed by 2,171 in the 2000s. Records show 1,133 in the 2010s and 858 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, so its total is not directly comparable with a finished decade.

The most active drillers in the records are Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) with 1,190, American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.) with 893, and Finney Drilling (Finney, Larry D.) with 731.

Those are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. When gathering bids around Cañon City, Rockvale or Williamsburg, ask about recent work in comparable ground and request a written explanation of what the drilling price includes.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Fremont's Mountain Bedrock
sections.html:
The supplied drilling model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At Fremont County's 182 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $11,800–$18,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $17,800–$30,200.

Treat that as a planning range, not a parcel quote. The 80–320 ft middle-half depth range leaves plenty of room for the footage charge to change. Access, casing and grout requirements, pump selection and the route to the house also affect the scope.

Have the bid separate drilling from completion work and explain how additional depth is authorized. On a steep lot near Coaldale or Howard, settle rig access and utility routing before relying on the finished-well estimate.

sections.heading: Mine Features, Water Quality and Low-Yield Risk
sections.html:
The environmental map includes 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 404 historic mine features and 20 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features are reasons to investigate a parcel, not evidence that its well water is contaminated. A sampling location also does not automatically mean contamination was detected.

Before buying, obtain laboratory testing appropriate to drinking-water use and the property's setting. Ask the testing professional whether nearby mine features or cleanup records call for additional analyses.

Water quantity needs its own check. Fractured bedrock can produce a weak well or a dry hole despite a productive neighbor. Review casing and grout records, and coordinate the well location with septic design, drainage, building placement and equipment access before committing to a site plan.

sections.heading: Before You Buy a Lot in Penrose, Cotopaxi or Beyond
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, well completion report and pump record. Confirm that the documents describe the well actually serving the property and that authorized uses match your plans. A well permit is not, by itself, proof of a completed or dependable supply.

Next, compare nearby wells in the same terrain. The 182 ft county median is useful background, but records close to your lot in Penrose, Lincoln Park or Cotopaxi are more relevant than a countywide average. Look at depth, yield and the dates and conditions of testing together.

For vacant land, confirm permit eligibility with DWR before purchase. Household-use restrictions or augmentation requirements may affect the plan. Lay out the well, septic system, driveway and house together rather than treating water as an issue to solve after construction starts.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fremont County, Colorado?
faq.a: Fremont County wells reporting depth have a median of 182 ft, with the middle half between 80 and 320 ft. The 90th percentile is 500 ft. Fractured bedrock makes depth unpredictable, so use nearby completion reports to set a bidding range rather than assuming your well will stop at the county median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fremont County?
faq.a: The local bedrock drilling model is $65–$100 per foot. At the 182 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $11,800–$18,200, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $17,800–$30,200. Your quote should address additional footage, casing and grout, access and the connection to the house.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Fremont County?
faq.a: County permit records cannot establish drinking-water safety for a particular well. The environmental map includes 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 404 historic mine features and 20 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Proximity does not prove contamination. Obtain laboratory testing and use nearby environmental records to help determine which additional contaminants should be checked.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Fremont County?
faq.a: Among 3,276 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gpm and the middle half is 4.5–10.0 gpm. The records show 3% under 1 gpm. Before buying, have the well's pumping performance and recovery evaluated; an old reported yield does not guarantee the supply will meet your household's current demands.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Fremont County?
faq.a: The recorded median static level was 38 ft below ground in the 1970s and 100 ft in the 2020s, but intervening decades do not show a steady decline. These are different sets of wells and measurements, not a consistent monitoring network. The series warrants local investigation but cannot establish a falling water table beneath your parcel.
